experiments.name: rk to flags chain
experiments.init: li.d $r12, 5; li.d $r13, 7; li.d $r14, 9; li.d $r15, 11; armmtflag $r12, 0xff; x86mtflag $r12, 0x3f
experiments.command: ./bench --method slope --unroll 20000 --unroll2 40000 --iters 100 --warmup 10 --reps 10 --init 'li.d $r12, 5; li.d $r13, 7; li.d $r14, 9; li.d $r15, 11; armmtflag $r12, 0xff; x86mtflag $r12, 0x3f' --asm 'armadc.w $r12, $r13, 14; armmfflag $r13, 0xff'

latencies.notes: rk -> ARMFLAGS: the chain closes through `armmfflag` writing rk back from the flags, so the measured 4.00 cycles less the 2-cycle flag move leave 2, the same as the rj path.

notes: LBT ARM-style instruction. Latency is recorded for each source operand: ARMFLAGS -> ARMFLAGS (1), rj -> ARMFLAGS (3). Only ARMFLAGS is written: the general-purpose registers are read-only sources for this instruction (verified with a native test program, where armadd.w, armsub.w, armand.w, armmov.w, armrotr.w and armrrx.w leave every GPR unchanged while ARMFLAGS changes; the conditional move armMove is the exception and does write its destination). Throughput is not measurable for this instruction: it reads and writes the architectural flag register, so every copy depends on the flags written by the previous one and a body of copies is a dependency chain, not a set of independent lanes. Eight copies take 16 cycles, which is exactly the 2-cycle read-modify-write latency, so the only number that can be quoted is that a stream of flag-modifying instructions runs at one per two cycles. The `throughput` array is therefore empty; see the latency entry from EFLAGS to EFLAGS.
